title: Words from German
kidRule: Some English words came from German. German loves the letters K and Z, spells the 'ts' sound with a Z, as in WALTZ, and often sticks two smaller pieces together to make one long word, as in HAMBURGER!
hint: This word came from German! Listen for a strong K or a 'ts' sound, and see if you can hear two smaller pieces joined together.
reminder: German words like the letter K, and they spell the 'ts' sound with Z or T-Z. Long ones are smaller pieces joined together, so spell one piece at a time.

check.question: Why does WALTZ end with the letters T-Z?
check.correctAnswer: It came from German, where the 'ts' sound is spelled with a Z!
distractors: Because every dance word ends with the letter Z
Because the letter S is never allowed at the end of a word

words.def: A round patty of cooked meat served inside a soft bun.
words.sent: I put pickles on my hamburger.
words.story: The hamburger is named after Hamburg, a city in Germany. There is no ham in it at all!
words.card: Silly me, there is no *ham* in a *hamburger*, only in my pocket!

words.def: A smooth, gliding dance for two people, counted one-two-three.
words.sent: Grandma and Grandpa danced a waltz in the kitchen.
words.story: This word comes from the German 'walzen', which means to roll or turn, because the dancers turn around and around!
words.card: The *wal*rus danced a wobbly *waltz* on the ice!

words.def: A small furry pet with cheek pouches for carrying food.
words.sent: My hamster runs on its wheel at night.
words.story: This word comes from German. A hamster can stuff so much food into its cheek pouches that its head looks twice as wide!
words.card: I *am* sure my *hamster* is hiding a peanut in each cheek!

words.def: To sing by switching quickly between a low voice and a very high voice.
words.sent: The farmer began to yodel across the valley.
words.story: Long ago, herders in the Alps would yodel to call to each other from one mountain to the next!
words.card: The *yo*-yo champion can *yodel* and do tricks at the same time!

words.def: A bag with two straps that you carry on your back.
words.sent: I packed a snack and a map in my rucksack.
words.story: In German, 'Rücken' means back and 'Sack' means bag, so a rucksack is a back-bag!
words.card: My *rucksack* is really a *sack* full of sandwiches for the ducks!

words.def: A pastry made of thin, flaky layers rolled around a sweet filling such as apples.
words.sent: We shared a warm apple strudel for dessert.
words.story: In German, strudel means whirlpool, because the rolled-up pastry makes a swirl when you slice it!
words.card: It is *rude* to eat the whole *strudel* before the guests sit down!

words.def: A hard, shiny mineral that is often clear like glass.
words.sent: I found a sparkly piece of quartz on the beach.
words.story: This word came from German miners. Quartz is one of the most common minerals on Earth, and a lot of beach sand is made of tiny bits of it!
words.card: My *art* project is a lump of *quartz* wearing googly eyes!

words.def: Cabbage cut into thin strips and left to turn sour.
words.sent: Grandpa piles sauerkraut on his hot dog.
words.story: In German, 'sauer' means sour and 'Kraut' means cabbage, so sauerkraut is simply sour cabbage!
words.card: The dino*sau*r ate a whole barrel of *sauerkraut* and made a sour face!

words.def: A dark, heavy bread made from rye.
words.sent: She made a cheese sandwich on pumpernickel bread.
words.story: Pumpernickel comes from Germany, where the bread is baked very slowly for many hours until it turns dark brown and a little bit sweet!
words.card: I paid one *nickel* for a slice of *pumpernickel* as big as my head!

words.def: A small dog with a very long body and very short legs.
words.sent: The dachshund trotted along on its short legs.
words.story: In German, 'Dachs' means badger and 'Hund' means dog. These little dogs were bred long ago to follow badgers into their burrows!
words.card: One *hund*red sweaters, and not one is long enough for my *dachshund*!
